episode.throughLine: Returning to school with little money, a woman completed preparatory work while accepting help with employment, clothing and the next stage of study.

contentProfile.contentNote: Poverty, interrupted education and uncertainty about belonging, with practical support from teachers and classmates.

facts.statement: Hurston was born January 7, 1891; the estate chronology places Morgan Academy attendance from September 1917 to June 1918, making her twenty-six on entry.
Hurston recalled that after unsuccessful attempts to save enough money and with her clothes nearly gone, she attended night high school.

sourceRefs.locator: IX School Again, paragraph beginning 'How then did I get back to school?'

facts.statement: In night school she submitted written work and answered questions; Holmes read a poem, complimented her work after class, and she went to Morgan to register the following week. She returned to the night class twice after the compliment.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, from 'I turned in written work' through 'went out to Morgan College to register'

facts.statement: She arrived expecting to be afraid of the dean; she had no money and no family to refer to, but he talked with her.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'William Pickens, a Negro, was the Dean there'

facts.statement: The dean gave her a brief examination, credited her with two years of high-school work, and assigned her to a class.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, same William Pickens paragraph, final two sentences

facts.statement: A few days later the dean's wife told her of a job helping an injured woman dress in the morning and undress at night; it provided a home and two dollars weekly.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, from 'Knowing that I had no money' through 'glad to accept the job'

facts.statement: Hurston accepted the job and lived in the household, where she read books from its library.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, 'So I went to live with the Baldwins' and next paragraph

facts.statement: At Morgan she had one dress, a change of underwear and one pair of tan shoes; she described herself as plain beside attractive classmates.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'And here I was, with my face'

facts.statement: She neither rushed to make friends nor withdrew. On her second day, a classmate quietly handed her a handkerchief in chapel; she nodded thanks.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'Therefore, I did not rush up to make friends'

facts.statement: She studied hard and said she felt behind; she specifically denied that classmates snubbed or pushed her around.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraphs beginning 'It would be dramatic' and 'Nobody shoved me around'

facts.statement: The estate's account says she declared herself sixteen, using a 1901 birth year, to qualify for free public schooling; no registration form or spoken exchange was inspected.

sourceRefs.locator: Biography paragraph beginning 'In 1917, she turned up in Baltimore'

facts.statement: After about a week at Morgan, Bernice Hughes watched her during English History with fixed eyes and a frown; Hurston did not know what to think and was doing well in recitation.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'One day, after about a week in school'

facts.statement: As the class moved to another room, Hughes joined her, praised her knowledge teasingly, and said she would sit beside her; both laughed.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, from 'When the period was over' through Hughes's next speech and 'So from then on'

facts.statement: Classmates offered to lend her clothes for events, approaching her or writing notes, and she accepted the offers in rotation.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'It soon became apparent that my lack of clothes'

facts.statement: Friends urged her to continue to Howard; Hughes offered a place in her family's home and help finding paid work; Hurston moved, worked and saved her first quarter's tuition.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, from friends' Howard discussion through 'went up to register'

facts.statement: At Howard she lacked money and needed additional preparatory work; Holmes encouraged her when she considered giving up, and she made up the missing hours.

sourceRefs.locator: IX, paragraph beginning 'Lo and behold, there was Dwight Holmes'

facts.statement: Hurston completed Morgan Academy's high-school requirements in June 1918, attended Howard Prep in 1918-19, and entered Howard University in 1919.
Zora Neale Hurston was a writer who wrote the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God.
Hurston died in 1960 with too little money for her own funeral; neighbors took up a collection and her grave was initially unmarked.

sourceRefs.locator: Biography, death and burial paragraphs before Alice Walker's search

arc.canonicalText: She came to the school to register, with no money to pay her way. She was twenty-six. In her memory, the dean talked with her when she arrived. She had been taking classes at night. There she had submitted written work and answered questions with the other students. An English teacher had stopped her after class to praise her work. She had returned to his class twice after that. Now she had come to enroll in a school where she could finish her education. She was there.
arc.sourceNote: Morgan registration, September 1917; memory cue covers the autobiography's encounter. Age is corrected using estate birth/enrollment dates. No invented office, clerk, registration form, dialogue or physical exchange of documents.

arc.canonicalText: She had arrived expecting to be frightened of the dean. She had no family she could refer him to. And she had no money. Before returning to school, she had tried to save enough to make it possible. The attempts had not brought her what she needed. Her clothes were almost gone when she finally went to the night classes. She had gone without waiting to gather enough money first. Now the dean had a woman before him who wanted to register and could not pay her way. She had come anyway.
arc.sourceNote: CRAFT HOLD: material pressure and anticipated fear are recollected context at registration, not a separately attested refusal or crisis in the dean's presence. No invented humiliation, hostile official, deadline or legal-age dialogue.

arc.canonicalText: She took the short examination the dean gave her. He credited her with two years of high-school work and assigned her to a class. A few days later, his wife sent for her. There was paid work that could fit around school. A woman with a broken hip needed help getting dressed in the morning and undressed at night. The job came with a place to live and a little weekly pay. She accepted it and moved into the household. There were books in its library. She began to read them.
arc.sourceNote: CRAFT HOLD: examination is a documented small act, but this passage compresses admission and subsequent job arrangements across several days. The memoir merely infers communication between the dean and his wife; that causal detail is omitted.

arc.canonicalText: At school she had one dress, one change of underwear, and one pair of shoes. Around her were classmates she thought pretty and well dressed. She felt plain among them. She did not rush forward to make friends, but she did not draw away either. On her second day, another girl quietly lent her a handkerchief during the school assembly. She nodded her thanks. She studied hard and felt behind. The age she had given for schooling was sixteen. Her actual age was ten years greater. But the pupils did not shove her aside or treat her as an outcast. She had classmates who helped her. She still had one dress.
arc.sourceNote: Material difficulty is retained without inventing peer cruelty, which Hurston explicitly denies. The estate supports the age deduction, not a witnessed clerk encounter. SOURCE QUALIFICATION: no contemporaneous age declaration inspected; memoir chronology differs from estate timeline.

arc.canonicalText: About a week into school, she noticed a girl watching her in history class. The girl's eyes stayed on her, and her lips were drawn into a frown. She did not know what to think. She liked the subject and was doing well when called on to answer. When the class ended, the students moved toward another room. The girl fell into step beside her. She teased her about how much she knew and gave her a nickname for it. Then she said she was going to sit beside her. She joked that there was no need for both of them to study. They laughed together.
arc.sourceNote: Single transition out of history class, from Hurston's later memory. Dialogue is paraphrased without quotation marks. No inferred hostile motive for the frown, no invented realization, and no claim that one encounter alone enabled all subsequent study.

arc.canonicalText: Her classmates began offering clothes for school events. They came up to her or sent notes, and she took turns accepting their offers. She completed the high-school requirements. Friends wanted her to continue studying and offered practical help. The girl from history class offered a place in her family's home and help finding a job. She moved, worked, and gathered enough money for her first term. But at the next school she was short of money again and needed additional preparatory work. She nearly gave up. Her former night-school teacher was there and encouraged her. She stayed and made up the work. There were more classes ahead.
arc.sourceNote: Ends with the 1918-19 preparatory transition, within the released 1917-21 episode; age range truthfully narrows to 26-28. No Barnard, writing fame or legacy list. Memoir's 'two years at Morgan' conflicts with 1917-18 chronology and is not adopted.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Zora Neale Hurston.

She wrote the novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you. You are allowed to want something you have wanted for a long time. You do not have to be early.
arc.sourceNote: Identity and book title only here; the estate supports authorship. Reader lines give no instruction or prediction.

dramatizationLimits: Do not invent a registration clerk, age declaration scene, documents, classroom gestures or quotes.
Retrospective memoir scenes remain probable; date and age corrections are explicitly identified.
Do not transform practical assistance into a claim that one person rescued her or made the career possible.
avoidRules: Keep names, calendar years, cities and institutions anonymous until the bridge.
Do not repeat the memoir's altered age as actual age.
Do not assert the exact under-twenty Maryland eligibility rule without a primary legal record.
Do not depict classmates as cruel or dismissive; Hurston explicitly rejects that version.
Retain the source and craft qualifications until independent review.
